title: Eurozone Growth Stalls at 0.4% as France Contracts, Leaving Lagarde's Successor a Divided Currency Bloc
subhead: Eurostat's flash estimate put euro-area third-quarter GDP growth at 0.4%, with France shrinking 0.1%, two days after the ECB held rates at 2.5% and Christine Lagarde announced she will leave on 7 February 2027, opening the succession at a moment when French debt is setting the bloc's borrowing costs.

sections.heading: Eurozone Growth Cools to 0.4% and France Goes Into Reverse
sections.body:
Eurostat's preliminary flash estimate, published Friday 30 October, put seasonally adjusted third-quarter GDP growth at +0.4% in the euro area and +0.5% across the EU, down from 0.6% and 0.7% in the second quarter. Year over year the euro area grew 1.3%. The composition is the story: France contracted 0.1% on the quarter, Lithuania fell 1.0%, and Germany managed only +0.2%. Ireland (+5.5%) and Spain (+0.6%) carried the aggregate for the second consecutive quarter.

This is the first hard output number to land after the ECB's decision day, and it undercuts the argument that the energy shock is purely an inflation problem. The bloc is growing at roughly half the pace of its own second quarter while headline inflation sits at 3.8%, and its two largest economies are contributing almost nothing. Germany at +0.2% is especially weak given the scale of the defence and infrastructure spending that was supposed to be lifting it.
sections.whyItMatters: Stagnation plus 3.8% inflation boxes the ECB in: it cannot cut into an energy shock and is reluctant to hike into a 0.2% German economy. The 'stagflation but no recession' baseline gets harder to defend each quarter.

sections.heading: Lagarde's Early Exit Hands the Succession to Capitals, Not the Governing Council
sections.body:
On Thursday 29 October, hours before the rate decision, the ECB announced that Christine Lagarde will leave on 7 February 2027, roughly nine months before her eight-year term expires in October 2027, according to Euronews. Lagarde said she was going so she would have 'greater freedom to express her views and to engage in non-monetary matters' and that she could 'not remain neutral' about developments in France and the world.

The timing is explicitly political. Euronews reports that the early departure was designed to let Macron and Chancellor Friedrich Merz settle the appointment before France's April 2027 presidential election, in which the far-right Rassemblement National polls strongly. The frontrunners are Pablo Hernández de Cos, the former Bank of Spain governor now running the BIS, backed by Madrid in July, and Klaas Knot, the former Dutch central bank chief. Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel is also mentioned, though Germany has never held the post.

This is not a single vacancy. Isabel Schnabel leaves on 3 January 2027 to join the IMF, and chief economist Philip Lane's term ends 31 May 2027 — three of the six Executive Board seats turn over within five months, and Euronews reports capitals expect to negotiate them as a package. The deadline for Schnabel's seat was extended to 27 November.
sections.whyItMatters: The next ECB president will be chosen by a qualified majority of leaders who are hedging against a eurosceptic French government, not primarily on monetary doctrine. Package-trading three board seats raises the odds of a compromise candidate whose views on TPI and the bond run-off are unknown — precisely when French spreads are doing the ECB's tightening for it.

sections.heading: The ECB Holds at 2.5% While French Yields Run the Policy
sections.body:
The Governing Council left the deposit rate at 2.5% on Thursday, with the main refinancing rate at 2.65% and the marginal lending facility at 2.90%, after two hikes this year, the last in September, per Euronews. The statement flagged energy prices that had 'continued to rise, posing upside risks to the inflation outlook and downside risks to the growth outlook', acknowledged financing conditions 'have tightened since the Governing Council's last meeting', and repeated that the ECB is 'not pre-committing to a particular rate path'.

The market backdrop matters more than the hold. French 10-year yields climbed above 5% last week for the first time since 2002 and stood near 5% on Thursday with a spread of roughly 155bp over Bunds, per Euronews. ING estimated the yield rise since September had done the work of a 25bp hike in Germany and closer to 50bp in France, concluding that 'the bond market has taken over the ECB's job'. Lagarde has refused to pre-commit to a rescue, saying in Bangkok that 'the primary and first solution lies at home in France'. The ECB nonetheless repeated that its never-used Transmission Protection Instrument remains available, and kept shrinking its balance sheet by not reinvesting maturing debt.
sections.whyItMatters: A single hold is unremarkable; the fact that French fiscal risk is importing 50bp of tightening into the eurozone's second-largest economy is not. The ECB has a tool it has never fired and a president with 14 weeks left — the gap between the two is the eurozone's actual policy risk this winter.

sections.heading: Energy Is Doing the Inflation Work: Eurozone Energy Prices Up 14.3% Year on Year
sections.body:
Eurostat's August data, the latest full component breakdown, showed euro-area energy inflation at 14.3%, up from 10.3% in July, against headline of 3.3% in August rising to 3.8% in September per Euronews. Stripping out energy, inflation is 2.2%; services ran 3.0% in August, down from 3.3% in July, and non-energy industrial goods just 1.2%.

That split is the whole argument inside the Governing Council. Core is at or near target and services are decelerating — a case for looking through the shock. But energy is climbing at double digits with a two-month lag on crude, and Brent has been trading above $110 on the Iran war and Gulf shipping risk. France's own HICP was only 2.7% in August against Spain's 4.5% and Lithuania's 5.8%, which means the inflation problem and the fiscal problem are concentrated in different countries.
sections.whyItMatters: The eurozone does not have one inflation problem; it has an energy-price problem that lands hardest on import-dependent peripherals and a fiscal problem that lands entirely on France. A single deposit rate cannot address both, and the divergence is politically corrosive inside a bloc that is already negotiating its central bank's leadership.

sections.heading: The Fed Held at 10-2 and Cut Its Own Meeting Calendar
sections.body:
The FOMC voted on Wednesday 28 October to keep rates at 3.75% to 4% in its last decision before the 3 November midterms, despite inflation rising from 3.4% in August to 3.7% in September, per NBC News. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favour of a hike — Cook's first dissent since joining in 2022, and notable given Trump's attempt to remove her. Chairman Kevin Warsh also announced the Fed will reduce voting meetings from eight to seven in 2027 and by two more in 2028, saying the change would improve the 'quality' of decisions.

Warsh said energy and related prices 'have moved higher again in recent weeks' and that the Fed's job is to ensure 'relative price changes in some sectors do not broaden out across the economy'. The statement said economic activity is 'expanding at a strong pace' with 'resilient' domestic spending. Morgan Stanley read the language as a signal the Fed 'might not be done tightening'. Notably, the dissenters wanted to move before the data did — a hawkish signal about the December meeting.
sections.whyItMatters: Reducing the number of rate decisions is a structural change to how the Fed forms policy, made by a chairman under sustained political pressure, at a moment when two voters already think he is behind the curve. December is now the live meeting, and the Fed has fewer chances per year to correct a mistake.

sections.heading: The IMF Warns the Bond Market Itself Is Now the Systemic Risk
sections.body:
In its Global Financial Stability Report released at the Bangkok annual meetings, the IMF warned government bond yields could rise in a 'disorderly' fashion, per CNBC. It cited high debt loads and rollover risk that leave the bond market 'susceptible to more frequent fiscal and inflation shocks', and noted global public debt near its highest share of GDP since World War II and on track to exceed 100%. The IMF flagged two amplifiers: hedge funds now hold about 9% of US Treasuries, up from roughly 4% in 2022, largely through leveraged basis trades; and AI-related corporate issuance, where hyperscalers' share of global investment-grade issuance has gone from under 1% since 2024 to 10%, competing with governments for duration buyers.

The fund also warned about 'circular' AI financing: since 2023, 14 disclosed deals moved about $300 billion of equity and $650 billion of debt into weaker AI firms in exchange for $1.4 trillion of future revenue commitments. Japan was singled out as the exception on liquidity, with its government bond market having 'continued to deteriorate' since the end of yield curve control.
sections.whyItMatters: This reframes the risk: it is no longer only about a sovereign defaulting, but about the collateral plumbing underneath every other market. With Japan's JGB liquidity deteriorating and hedge-fund Treasury leverage doubled in three years, a shock in one bond market now transmits through margin calls rather than through credit events.

sections.heading: Washington and Mexico City Race the Midterms for a Tariff Deal
sections.body:
Mexico and the United States are accelerating talks toward an interim bilateral trade agreement before the 3 November midterms, according to reporting carried by Taiwan Sun. Mexico is seeking meaningful reductions in US tariffs on autos, steel and aluminium, and the package would address US concerns over automotive content rules and Chinese investment in Mexican industry. CSIS analysis notes that what Mexico concedes for tariff relief now 'could set the baseline for North America down the line'.

Separately, the sanctions landscape around Russia remains unsettled after Washington temporarily eased restrictions on Russian diesel following the Trump-Putin arrangement reported in early October, with CNBC noting criticism that the move contradicts existing Russia sanctions law.
sections.whyItMatters: An interim deal signed for electoral timing rather than structural resolution sets a precedent Mexico will be held to for years, and it would lock in automotive content rules aimed squarely at Chinese supply chains. For markets, the question is whether relief is durable past 3 November or reversible.

bottomLine: The week's defining number was not a rate decision but 0.4%: euro-area growth halved in the third quarter while France contracted outright, two days after the ECB held at 2.5% with inflation at 3.8% and its president announced she is leaving in February. Lagarde's early exit is deliberately timed to let Paris and Berlin pick her successor before France's April 2027 election, and with Schnabel and Lane also departing, half the Executive Board turns over within five months — a leadership vacuum arriving exactly as French 10-year yields near 5% do the tightening the ECB will not. Across the Atlantic the Fed held at 3.75-4% on a 10-2 vote with two members wanting a hike, and Chairman Warsh cut the number of policy meetings, a change to the institution itself rather than to policy. The IMF's warning that Treasury and JGB markets are now the systemic weak point, with hedge funds holding 9% of Treasuries and AI issuers taking 10% of investment-grade supply, describes the channel through which any of these stresses would actually spread. Watch 27 November, the extended deadline for the Schnabel seat, and the December FOMC.
sources: Eurostat, Euronews, NBC News, CNBC, IMF Global Financial Stability Report, ING, Morgan Stanley, CSIS, Taiwan Sun
